title: About — BareBoard
text: About At Bareboard, our mission is to behave as a free educational and beneficial platform. Offering anyone unprecedented access to educational resources, providing people the opportunity to take back their power individually, collectively, and simply. Organized at the scale of a corporation and delivered individually. How we work Responsible disclosure first. Manufacturers hear about a finding before the public does. Nothing weaponizable. We never publish weaponizable material or reconstructed commercial firmware in ways that could put people at risk. Verified findings only. Every claim is backed by our own hardware, our own bench, our own captures. Where something is uncertain, we date it and mark it — never hide it. Free, no paywall. Education that charges admission isn’t education, it’s a gate. Open hardware allies. We stand with the open-source hardware movement — see the Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA) . What this is not BareBoard is not a hacking collective, not a leak site, and not a shortcut around anyone’s security. It is a bench, a notebook, and a publishing desk — in that order. title: Support — BareBoard
text: Support BareBoard Free for readers, funded by readers. No paywall, no ads, no selling data — this is the budget line that keeps it that way. A note from the bench We started BareBoard on a simple belief: education should be a human right — free and free to access. Everything here will always be free to read. No paywall, no premium tier, no exceptions. Free to read doesn’t mean free to run. The bench needs devices to tear down, probes and adapters to measure them with, and a domain to live on. If this site ever taught you something, chip in and keep it running for the next person. Chip in Everything here is free and stays free — that’s the whole point. But free to read isn’t free to run: the bench needs devices to open, probes to measure them with, and a domain to live on. If BareBoard ever taught you something, saved you a repair bill, or just fed your curiosity — you can feed the parts jar. Any amount, one-time or monthly, entirely your call. And if money’s tight, sending the site to one curious person does just as much. Where it goes Bench devices. Teardowns need hardware — the rarer the device, the more it costs to get one onto the bench. Test equipment. Probes, adapters, and bench gear that make the findings possible. Domain & hosting. The unglamorous cost of staying online. A donation buys no influence. Findings are published on the evidence — never on who’s paying. BareBoard — a free educational resource. title: The BareBoard Hot 100™ — Free Hardware Education
text: Preliminary — methodology v0.1 The BareBoard Hot 100™ The 100 most-used consumer electronic devices overall — ranked #1 through #100 across a 1,000-device universe (top 100 in each of ten categories). Recomputed whenever the universe updates. #1 isn’t forever — it’s whoever matters most right now. How it’s ranked: 55% all-time units sold (log-scaled, confidence-weighted: A counts full, B at 75%, C at 50%, undisclosed scores zero — no invented numbers) + 45% still in use right now. The heat component (CVE severity × still deployed) folds in as vulnerability data lands per device. The data gap, quantified: ~70% of the 1,000-device universe has no public sales figure. Consoles and phones are the only categories with real numbers; IoT, networking, streamers, cameras and wearables are near-total black holes. The industry’s most-installed devices are its least-counted. Full per-category top-100 lists and sources available on request — every figure carries its source and confidence grade. Corrections welcome, verified corrections only. BareBoard — a free educational resource. Text and findings published under open terms; nothing here is for sale. When a device is acquired, it graduates off the board and the next one moves up. The ranking Score = 0.5 × Rarity + 0.3 × Darkness + 0.2 × Reach, each scored 0–10. Recomputed whenever the device universe updates or a bounty is claimed. The board Board opens with the 1,000-device universe. Rarity research is running now across all ten categories. The first ten bounties post here when the data lands. Have one of these on a shelf? Sourcing is handled privately while the program takes shape — no public intake yet. text: Xfinity XB3 (Arris TG1682G) Autopsy Report — BareBoard Device #001 Before you read anything else: what the FCC found Every wireless device sold legally in the United States must be tested and authorized by the Federal Communications Commission before it ships. That authorization is public record. This box has three: What the FCC filings contain and what they don't. The UIDTG1682-3 internal photos document covers the TG1682G/CT 4-port DOCSIS 3.0 Gateway made by ARRIS Group, Inc. Those FCC internal photos — available as a public PDF at the link above — were shot in late 2015. The board photographed in the FCC filing is an earlier board revision than the 2017 board documented here. Architecture is consistent; component placement and silkscreen markings differ. Treat the FCC photos as architectural reference, not as a match to this specific unit. Grantee code UID. ARRIS's FCC grantee code is UID. All ARRIS radio device applications are indexed under this code at the FCC's equipment authorization database. What the FCC authorization tells you as a hardware owner. The authorization certifies that the device's radio emissions stay within legal limits. It is not a statement about software behavior, remote management, or what traffic the device sends home. Those are separate questions that the FCC does not answer. This page tries to answer them from the hardware side. What this thing is The XB3 is the box Comcast handed to millions of internet customers. Its real name is the Arris TG1 FCC ID Filing variant Authorization date Filing link UIDTG1682 Original TG1682G — 4-port DOCSIS 3.0 Gateway 2014 fccid.io/UIDTG1682 UIDTG1682-2 TG1682G/CT revision — Touchstone Wireless Telephony Gateway 2014 fccid.io/UIDTG1682-2 UIDTG1682-3 TG1682G/CT further revision — 4-port DOCSIS 3.0 Gateway December 2015 fccid.io/UIDTG1682-3 Field Data Manufacturer Intel Part number DHCE2652 (S R278 stepping) Family / codename Intel Puma 6 / "Cat Mountain D0" Architecture Dual-core Intel Atom (x86) + ARM Cortex-A9 companion core Clock speed DHCE2652 runs at 1.2 GHz; it is a Home Gateway (24×8) variant of the Puma 6 family SoC. DOCSIS capability Supports bonding of up to 32 downstream and 8 upstream channels, delivering data rates exceeding 1 Gbps on DOCSIS 3.0 networks. The TG1682G is configured for 24×8. Introduced 2013 Confidence Confirmed — boot log names Puma 6; part number from public hardware records and this board family Why two cores? Besides a slightly faster ARM core, Intel added a dual-core Atom, so the chip runs two Linux instances. This was necessary since the TI DOCSIS stack was written for the ARM core. The Atom cores run the routing/application software; the ARM core runs the legacy cable modem DOCSIS stack. Puma family lineage The Puma series runs: Puma 4 (TNETC 4700/4710, DOCSIS 2.0), Puma 5 (TNETC 4800/4810, DOCSIS 3.0, 400 MHz ARMv6), Puma 6 (DHCE2652, DOCSIS 3.0, 450 MHz ARMv7 + 600/1200 MHz Atom), Puma 7 (FHCE2712/2752, DOCSIS 3.1). The Puma 5 was the last development by Texas Instruments before they sold their Cable Modem Unit to Intel. The original TI chips were named TNETC4800; Intel renamed them DNCE2500 after the purchase. Known defect CVE-2017-5693 — periodic high-latency spikes under mixed traffic loads. Two firmware updates from Intel did not fully resolve it. Intel formal advisory: August 2018. Datasheet status Intel does not publish a public consumer datasheet for the DHCE2652. Intel's Material Declaration Data Sheet (MDDS) is publicly available: Intel MDDS for Puma 6 family . Full technical datasheet is OEM/NDA-gated. No public equivalent exists. Archive.org sweep: no cached version located. Community chip database DevIWiki — Intel Puma · BoxMatrix — Puma 6 · CPU Grave Yard — DHCE2652 Field Data Manufacturer Samsung Part family K4B2G1646B Capacity 256 MB total (two 128 MB packages, package-on-package or side-by-side) Type LPDDR3 Confidence Confirmed — boot log on this unit reports DRAM: 256 MB Datasheet Samsung K4B2G1646B family datasheet (PDF) — Samsung Semiconductor · Archive.org cached copy: web.archive.org Field Data Label on board MMC256 Usable capacity reported by boot log 231.3 MB Type eMMC (embedded MultiMediaCard) Boot partition root=/dev/mmcblk0p5 (reported by this unit's boot log) Confidence Confirmed — boot log on this unit reports Flash: 0 kB (no raw NAND) and boots from eMMC. Public hardware records for this model family list a 128 MB raw NAND chip; this 2017 board uses eMMC instead. This was settled by listening to this unit's actual hardware. Note on public records discrepancy Earlier FCC teardown photos and pre-2017 public hardware database entries list a raw NAND flash chip for the TG1682G family. This 2017 board revision (REV G) replaced it with eMMC. If you are reading an older teardown, its storage section does not apply to this board revision. Datasheet eMMC standard: JEDEC JESD84-B51 (eMMC 5.1). Public download: jedec.org/standards-documents/docs/jesd84-b51 Field Data Manufacturer Qualcomm Atheros (acquired from Atheros Communications by Qualcomm, 2011) Part number AR9381 (variant AL1A) Package QFN-40 package, specified over the extended temperature range of -40°C to 105°C. Standard 802.11b/g/n (2.4 GHz) Confidence Likely — consistent across multiple public hardware databases for this model; chip is under a soldered RF shield. Shield was not removed. Datasheet status Qualcomm does not publish a public datasheet for the AR9381. The AR9381 FCC module reference appears in public FCC applications. Archive.org: no complete datasheet cached. Product listing with package/temperature specs: veswin.com/product-AR9381-AL1A.html Community database BoxMatrix — AR9381-AL1A Field Data Manufacturer Qualcomm Atheros Part number QCA9880 Standard 802.11a/n/ac (5 GHz), 3×3 MIMO Confidence Likely — consistent across multiple public hardware databases for this model; chip is under a soldered RF shield. Shield was not removed. Datasheet status Qualcomm does not publish a public datasheet for the QCA9880. The reference module manual submitted to the FCC for a QCA9880-based module is publicly available: FCC reference module filing Open-source driver Linux kernel driver ath10k supports QCA9880. Source: kernel.org ath10k documentation Field Data Manufacturer Broadcom Part number BCM53124S Port count 5-port (4 user-facing + 1 uplink to SoC) Speed Gigabit (10/100/1000 Mbps per port) Confidence Likely — consistent across public hardware databases for this model Datasheet Broadcom BCM53124 datasheet (PDF) — publicly available: search Broadcom's legacy product archive · Archive.org cached copy: web.archive.org — search BCM53124 Field Data Function Electrical isolation between the RJ-45 jacks and the switch chip. One transformer assembly per port. Blocks DC and high-voltage surges from entering the PCB. Date code on this unit 1741 (week 41 of 2017 — manufactured approximately 5 weeks before the board itself) Confidence Confirmed — read directly from date code on this unit Standard reference IEEE 802.3 specifies transformer isolation requirements for Ethernet physical layers. IEEE 802.3 standard — ieee.org Field Data Manufacturer Texas Instruments Part number TPS54328 Function Step-down (buck) voltage regulator feeding the Wi-Fi radio modules. 8-pin SOIC/MSOP package. Enable pin on Pin 8. Why this matters A published hardware modification for the XB3's bridge-mode radio interference problem targets this chip: grounding the enable pin (Pin 8) cuts power to the Wi-Fi radios while the modem and wired network continue to function. The board carries two shielded Atheros Wi-Fi modules fed by an 8-pin TPS54328 buck regulator. This report documents the mod as reference. We did not perform it on this unit. title: AI Crawler Defense — BareBoard
text: ← About BareBoard AI Crawler Defense How BareBoard keeps training scrapers off its work BareBoard publishes original hardware research — teardowns, measurements, photography — for humans learning hardware. AI training crawlers are not our audience, and we do not consent to feeding them. This page documents the layered defense we run. It is all boundary-setting, no trickery: nothing here deceives, traps, or poisons anyone. The problem Our content is expensive to produce — bench time, hardware, photography, careful documentation — and trivially cheap to scrape. Training crawlers ingest it into models that then compete with the free resource they learned from. We want search engines, because humans find us through search. We do not want training ingestion. Those are different crawlers with different purposes, and we treat them differently. Layer 1: robots.txt hardening The perimeter. Our robots.txt names the known AI training user-agents one by one and denies them the whole site, while the wildcard rule leaves the door open for everyone else — including Google and Bing, which is how humans discover us.
